summary: Give the Standard deviation index calculator the consensus group mean, the consensus group standard deviation and the standard deviation index and it returns laboratory mean. It is built for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Standard deviation index calculator work?
sections.html:
The Standard deviation index calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports laboratory mean in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the consensus group mean, the consensus group standard deviation and the standard deviation index (SDI).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Standard deviation index calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Laboratory mean=consensus group mean + consensus group standard deviation × standard deviation index (SDI)
Abs sdi=the absolute value of (standard deviation index (SDI))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Consensus group mean = 10, Consensus group standard deviation = 10 and Standard deviation index (SDI) = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Laboratory mean = 110 and Abs sdi = 10.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Laboratory mean = 110 and Abs sdi = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Consensus group mean = 10 and Consensus group standard deviation = 10.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Standard deviation index calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the consensus group mean, the consensus group standard deviation and the standard deviation index — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Standard deviation index calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — consensus group mean for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Standard deviation index calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns laboratory mean, derived from the consensus group mean, the consensus group standard deviation and the standard deviation index. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Standard deviation index calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the consensus group mean, the consensus group standard deviation and the standard deviation index, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Laboratory mean = 110. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Standard deviation index calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
